deep.reconstruction:
The page is a raw observing log from a transit instrument (Passageninstrument), not a mathematical derivation. It records two transits of the Pole Star α Ursae minoris over the seven threads (Fäden) of the reticle. The date is 'Oct. 11'; the weekday sign looks like ♀ (Friday).

(A) Upper culmination (O.C.), threads 1–7:
0h48'30", 0h55'24", 1h2'12", 1h9'8", 1h15'51", 1h22'47", 1h29'31".

(B) Lower culmination (U.C.), the same evening/night, threads 1–7:
12h48'0", 12h54'45", 13h1'40", 13h8'20", 13h15'22", 13h22'5", 13h29'0".

At the top a separate note gives '1. Fd. 0h 49' 14"'; this is perhaps an earlier or trial setting for thread 1. Under column A, 'ν Piscium' is evidently the next star to be observed. Its right ascension is about 1h34m, so it follows Polaris on the clock. The figures '10,7 / 10,8' and '22,2' are isolated jottings whose meaning I cannot determine.

Reduction (mine, not on the page):
- The thread intervals are about 6m50s. Total span thread 1→7: U.C. 2460 s; O.C. 2461 s, essentially identical.
- For Polaris, sec δ ≈ 40 (the next page has δ ≈ 88°34'). That gives an equatorial thread interval of about 2460/6/40 ≈ 10.2 s of time.
- Mean of the seven threads, O.C.: 0h48'00" + 8843/7 s = 1h9'3.3".
- Mean of the seven threads, U.C.: 12h48'00" + 8592/7 s = 13h8'27.4".
- The difference is 11h59'24.1", i.e. 35.9 s short of 12h.
- The clock is evidently sidereal: Polaris's right ascension is about 1h06m, so the clock reads about +3 min fast.
- In the classical reduction (Mayer's formula), the departure of the interval from 12h sidereal time is ≈ −2a·cosφ·tanδ + 2c·secδ + clock rate. Here a is the azimuth error and c the collimation error.
- The previous page determines the collimation. So these two culminations of Polaris serve to find the azimuth of the instrument, and/or to check the clock.
- The bare number '35' on the next page may be this ≈36 s.

The context (previous page: collimation of the Mittelfaden; next page: Polhöhe von Göttingen 51°31'48", settings for the Polarstern, refraction, index error) shows that the bundle records practical observatory work in Göttingen. These are instrument adjustment and latitude/time observations.
errors: No derivation errors possible: the page contains only raw thread times. The individual thread intervals scatter by about ±8 s (O.C.: 414, 408, 416, 403, 416, 404 s; U.C.: 405, 415, 400, 422, 403, 415 s). This is normal timing scatter for a star at sec δ≈40, i.e. about ±0.2 s equatorial.
Weekday check: 11 Oct was a Friday in 1850 and 1861, not 1859. So the '0859' at the top is presumably an archive number rather than the year, or the sign is not ♀. Dating is uncertain.

results.what: Seven-thread transit timings of Polaris at upper and lower culmination, to determine instrument azimuth / clock correction
results.modern_name: Transit-instrument reduction (Mayer/Bessel formula); azimuth from both culminations of a circumpolar star
results.usually_credited_to: Tobias Mayer (18th c.), Bessel (19th c. standard practice)

deep.surprise_reason: Purely routine observatory log with raw transit times. The only mild interest is documentary: it shows Riemann personally doing practical transit-instrument work, presumably at Göttingen. There is no mathematics on the page.

checkable.asserts: Mean of O.C. thread times, in seconds after 0h48m00s = 1263.29 s, i.e. mean transit 1h09m03.3s
Mean of U.C. thread times, in seconds after 12h48m00s = 1227.43 s, i.e. mean transit 13h08m27.4s
The interval between culminations falls short of 12h by about 35.9 s (it evaluates to approximately 35.86)
sec δ for δ=88°34'2" is approximately 40.0
Equatorial thread interval ≈ 10.25 s of time

transcription_corrections: Header '3. Fd.[?]' is more likely 'z. Fd.' or a marginal abbreviation; it is illegible.
The U.C. thread 7 hour should read 13h (13h29'0"); the scrawl resembles '10' but sequence demands 13.
U.C. thread 3 '1'40"' is consistent with the image ('13h 1'40"'); the hour is overwritten 12→13.
Upper-left 'g. 7. Min.' is uncertain; possibly 'g. 7. Mon.' or a note on clock correction.
